cards.title: Static Array vs Dynamic Array
cards.teaser: A static array is a fixed block of memory allocated at creation time. A dynamic array grows on demand — at the cost of an occasional O(n) copy that you almost never see in practice.

runs.text: A
static array

is a contiguous block of memory with a fixed size declared upfront. The size is baked in: if you need ten elements, you allocate ten slots, and that allocation never changes. C and C++ arrays are static. You get O(1) index access because the address of element i is just base_address + i * element_size, and every element is the same width.
The problem: you often don't know how many elements you'll have. This led to the
dynamic array

— an array that manages its own resizing. The backing store is still a static array under the hood, but when you append past the end, the dynamic array allocates a larger backing store, copies all existing elements, and frees the old one.

items.text: — size fixed at allocation; O(1) read/write by index; no allocation overhead after creation; wastes memory if you over-allocate or fails if you under-allocate.
— grows automatically; O(1) amortized append; O(n) copy on resize (rare); slightly more memory overhead from capacity tracking and the occasional half-used backing store.

runs.text: The key insight: the occasional O(n) resize is not a problem in practice because it happens so infrequently that the amortized cost per append is still O(1). Doubling (or near-doubling) the capacity each time is the mathematical reason this works.

Imagine reserving seats at a restaurant. A static array is calling ahead and booking exactly 8 seats — efficient if you're right, a problem if your group grows to 9. A dynamic array is a restaurant that says "we'll seat you, and if more friends show up we'll push tables together" — the occasional shuffle costs time, but you never get turned away.

cards.title: Python list — CPython Internals
cards.teaser: Python's list is a dynamic array of object pointers. Each slot holds a reference (8 bytes on 64-bit), not the object itself — which is why a list of ints uses far more memory than you'd expect.

runs.text: In CPython,
list
is implemented as a dynamic array of
PyObject*
pointers. The backing store is a C array of pointers, each 8 bytes wide on a 64-bit system. The actual Python objects live elsewhere on the heap — the list just holds references to them.
Three key fields live inside every list object:

items.text: — pointer to the backing array of PyObject* pointers.
— the number of elements currently stored (what
— the number of slots actually allocated in the backing array (capacity). Always >= ob_size.

runs.text: Because each slot is just a pointer, index access is O(1): dereference the pointer at offset i. Appending is O(1) amortized: write the pointer into the next slot if capacity allows; otherwise resize. The cost of indirection is that memory usage is higher than a typed array — a list of a million Python ints uses roughly 8 MB for the pointers alone, plus the overhead of each
int
object on the heap (28 bytes each in CPython for small ints not in the cache).
Run sys.getsizeof([]) to see the base list overhead (56 bytes on CPython 3.11+). It reports the size of the list shell and its pointer array, not the objects the list points to.

A Python list is like a corkboard covered in sticky notes where each sticky note has an address written on it. The corkboard itself is the dynamic array. The actual objects are somewhere else in the building. Looking up index 5 means reading the fifth sticky note and walking to that address — two hops instead of one, but the corkboard can grow without moving any of the objects.

cards.title: List Operation Complexities
cards.teaser: append is O(1) amortized. index access is O(1). insert and remove anywhere except the end are O(n) — every element after the target has to shift. This single fact explains most list performance bugs.

runs.text: Every list operation has a Big O cost you should be able to recite from memory:

items.text: (read or write by index) — O(1). Pointer arithmetic into the backing array.
— O(1) amortized. Write to the next slot if capacity allows; O(n) resize only when capacity is exhausted.
(pop from end) — O(1). Decrement length, no shifting.
(pop from index i) — O(n). Every element after index i shifts left by one.
— O(n). Every element at index i and beyond shifts right by one to make room.
— O(n). Linear scan to find x, then O(n) shift. Two linear passes in the worst case.
— O(1). The length is stored as a field, not computed by traversal.

runs.text: The classic performance mistake: calling lst.insert(0, x) or lst.pop(0) in a loop. Each call is O(n), so the loop is O(n²). If you need frequent front insertions or deletions, use collections.deque instead.

Appending to the end of a list is like adding a book to the right end of a shelf — just set it down. Inserting in the middle is like making room for a new book by physically sliding every book to the right of that spot one position over. The more books already on the shelf, the more sliding you do.

cards.title: Amortized O(1) Append — Growth Strategy
cards.teaser: CPython's list doesn't double on resize — it grows by roughly 1.125x (plus a small constant). The math still gives O(1) amortized append. Understanding why is the foundation for reasoning about any dynamic array.

runs.text: When a Python list's backing array is full and you call
append
, CPython computes a new capacity using the formula:

explanation.code:
new_allocated = ((size_t)newsize + (newsize >> 3) + 6) & ~(size_t)3
# newsize >> 3  is  newsize / 8  (roughly 12.5% growth)
# The & ~3 rounds down to a multiple of 4

runs.text: This gives roughly 1.125x growth (12.5% extra capacity), not the 2x doubling you see in textbooks or Java's
ArrayList
. The growth sequence for a list that starts empty and gets appended to: 0, 4, 8, 16, 25, 35, 46, 58, 72, 88, 106... CPython chose a gentler growth factor to reduce memory waste at large sizes.

Why is amortized O(1) still true despite the slower growth? The key is that any growth factor greater than 1 gives O(1) amortized cost. The proof: if you grow by factor k every time you hit capacity, the total copy work across n appends is bounded by a geometric series that sums to O(n), meaning O(1) per append on average. 1.125x grows the series more slowly than 2x, but the bound still holds.
The amortized argument only works for append (adding to the end). insert(0, x) does not benefit from amortization — it always shifts n elements and is genuinely O(n).

Imagine you're filling a hotel and every time it gets full you build a new, slightly bigger hotel and move everyone in. The moves are expensive, but they happen less and less often as the hotel grows. If you tally the total moving cost and divide by the number of guests ever hosted, each guest cost only a constant amount of moving work on average — that's what amortized O(1) means.

cards.title: List Slicing Complexity
cards.teaser: lst[a:b] is O(k) where k = b - a (the size of the slice), not O(1). A slice always allocates a new list and copies the pointers. Passing slices inside tight loops is a common source of hidden O(n²) behavior.

runs.text: Slicing a Python list with
lst[a:b]
creates a
new list object

and copies the pointers for the k = b - a elements in the requested range. The operation is O(k). The objects themselves are not copied — only the references. So the resulting slice shares the same underlying objects as the original list.
Common scenarios where slicing creates unexpected O(n) cost:

items.text: — passing lst[:mid] and lst[mid:] into recursive calls copies O(n) pointers at each level. Use index bounds instead.
Rolling window via slices in a loop
— taking lst[i:i+k] on every loop iteration copies k pointers each time. If both k and n are large, this is O(nk).
Clearing a list with lst = lst[1:]
in a loop — O(n²) total. Use
and popleft() for O(1) front removal.

explanation.code:
# O(n) slice — allocates a new list of n//2 pointers
half = lst[:n // 2]

# O(1) — no allocation; just record the index bounds
def merge_sort(lst, lo, hi): ...

runs.text: When you need a slice-like view without copying, pass (lst, lo, hi) index bounds, use a memoryview on a bytes/bytearray, or reach for NumPy which supports zero-copy views via stride tricks.

A list slice is like a photocopier, not a bookmark. When you ask for pages 10 to 20 of a document, a bookmark just remembers the page numbers (O(1)). A photocopier makes actual copies of those pages (O(k)). Python's slice is the photocopier. If you're in a hot loop, you want bookmarks.

cards.title: Singly Linked List
cards.teaser: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. O(1) prepend, O(1) delete-at-cursor — but O(n) index access and poor cache behavior make it lose to arrays in most practical benchmarks.

runs.text: A singly linked list stores data as a chain of
nodes
. Each node contains two fields: the data value and a
next
pointer to the following node. The last node's next pointer is None. The list maintains a head pointer (and optionally a tail pointer for O(1) append).
Complexity summary:

Cache behavior is the silent killer of linked list performance. Array elements are contiguous in memory — the CPU prefetcher loads them in bulk. Linked list nodes are scattered across the heap, causing cache misses on every node traversal. In practice, arrays outperform linked lists even for O(n) scans because of this locality advantage.

A singly linked list is like a treasure hunt where each clue tells you where the next clue is. To find clue number 7, you have to read clues 1 through 6 first — you can't jump directly. But adding a new first clue is instant: just write "go here first" on a new card and point it at the old first clue.

cards.title: Doubly Linked List
cards.teaser: A doubly linked list adds a prev pointer to each node, enabling O(1) deletion given only the node (no predecessor needed) and O(1) backward traversal. It's the structure behind collections.deque and Python's lru_cache internals.

runs.text: A doubly linked list extends the singly linked list by adding a
prev
pointer to each node alongside
next
. The list maintains both a head and a tail. This symmetry unlocks two capabilities:

items.text: O(1) delete given just the node
— rewire node.prev.next and node.next.prev; no predecessor search needed.
— appendleft and pop from either end without traversal.

explanation.code:
class DNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def unlink(node):      # O(1) — no predecessor search
    node.prev.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = node.prev

runs.text: The canonical real-world use of a doubly linked list is the
LRU cache

. When a cached item is accessed, it must be moved to the "most recently used" end of the eviction order in O(1). A doubly linked list lets you unlink any node in O(1) (because you have prev) and re-insert it at the head in O(1). Pair it with a hash map for O(1) lookup and you have a complete LRU cache.

Python's functools.lru_cache is implemented with a doubly linked list (stored as a circular list inside a Python list for cache efficiency) plus a dict. The doubly linked structure is what allows O(1) move-to-front on every cache hit.

A doubly linked list is like a two-way train: each car knows the car in front and the car behind. To remove a car from the middle of a singly linked train, you'd have to start from the engine and walk to find the car just before it. With two-way links, the car can tell the one behind it to connect directly to the one in front — no walking required.

cards.title: Linked List vs Array — When to Use Which
cards.teaser: Arrays win for random access, iteration, and memory efficiency. Linked lists win for O(1) insertion/deletion at a known position when you already hold a reference. In Python, the answer is almost always list or deque — not a custom linked list.

runs.text: The textbook trade-off:

items.text: when you need random access by index, when you iterate sequentially (cache locality matters), or when memory overhead per element must be low.
when you frequently insert or delete in the middle and already hold a cursor/pointer to the target position, avoiding the O(n) shift cost of arrays.

runs.text: In practice, the linked list case is rarer than textbooks suggest. Reasons:

items.text: — linked list nodes are heap-scattered; array elements are contiguous. For typical n in production code, array iteration is 5–10x faster in wall time even when both are O(n) theoretically.
— getting to the insertion point is O(n) if you don't already have a pointer. If you had to search first, you didn't save anything.
— each node is a full Python object (64+ bytes of overhead); arrays of pointers are far more compact.

runs.text: Interview answer: "Linked lists give O(1) insert/delete at a known position vs O(n) for arrays. In Python specifically, I'd use collections.deque for front/back operations rather than implementing a linked list manually, since deque is implemented in C and handles the cache-miss penalty." This answer is both correct and shows production awareness.

Arrays are like a row of numbered lockers — you can walk directly to locker 47 in one step, and all the lockers are right next to each other so you can quickly scan many in a row. Linked lists are like post-it notes scattered around an office, each with an arrow pointing to the next one. Following arrows is fine, but you can't jump to note 47 without following 46 arrows first, and the walking between notes wastes time.

cards.title: collections.deque
cards.teaser: deque ("deck") is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks, not a single linked list. It gives O(1) append and appendleft, O(1) pop and popleft — while keeping better cache behavior than a node-per-element linked list.

runs.text: Python's
collections.deque
is implemented in C as a doubly linked list of
fixed-size blocks

(64 slots each in CPython). Each block is a small array. Blocks are linked together, and the deque tracks a left-block/left-index and right-block/right-index for the two ends. This block structure gives deque better cache behavior than a pure node-per-element linked list while retaining O(1) operations at both ends.
Complexity:

items.text: — O(n). Must traverse blocks from the closer end.
— O(k). Moves k elements from one end to the other.

explanation.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque()          # use as a FIFO queue
queue.append('a')        # enqueue — O(1)
queue.append('b')
queue.popleft()          # dequeue — O(1)

stack = deque()          # also works as stack (but list is fine for stacks)
stack.append('x')
stack.pop()

runs.text: Use deque when you need O(1) operations at both ends. Use list when you only append/pop from the right end — list is faster for that use case because of better memory locality (one contiguous block vs block-linked structure). Never use list.pop(0) in a loop — that's O(n) per call.

A deque is like a queue of shopping carts where you can add or remove carts from either the front or the back instantly. The block-of-64 design means each "cart" actually holds 64 items, so you're not chasing a new pointer for every single element — you get some of the cache benefits of arrays while keeping both-ends-O(1) flexibility.

cards.title: Tuple vs List — Immutability and Memory
cards.teaser: Tuples are immutable, slightly smaller than lists, and hashable (so they can be dict keys or set members). Use tuple for fixed collections of heterogeneous data; use list for homogeneous sequences that will change.

runs.text: Both
list
and
tuple
are sequences of object references with O(1) index access. The core difference is mutability: tuples are immutable — you cannot add, remove, or replace elements after creation.
Memory: a tuple of n elements is smaller than a list of the same n elements because:

items.text: — a tuple allocates exactly n pointer slots, never more. A list over-allocates for future appends.
— the list object stores ob_size and allocated (capacity); the tuple only needs ob_size since it never changes.

explanation.code:
import sys
print(sys.getsizeof((1, 2, 3)))   # 72 bytes (CPython 3.11)
print(sys.getsizeof([1, 2, 3]))   # 88 bytes

# Tuples are hashable — usable as dict keys
coords = {(0, 0): 'origin', (1, 0): 'right'}

# Lists are not hashable
# {[0, 0]: 'origin'}  →  TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

runs.text: Convention: use tuples for semantically fixed groups (a coordinate pair, a database row, a return value with multiple fields) and lists for collections you intend to mutate or extend. Named tuples (
collections.namedtuple
or
typing.NamedTuple
) add field names without losing immutability or hashability.

A tuple is a sealed envelope: you decide the contents when you seal it, and nothing goes in or out afterward. A list is an open folder: you can add pages, remove pages, reorder them. The sealed envelope is slightly smaller because it doesn't need the extra space for a "how full is this thing" counter, and it can be used as a key in a filing system (dict key) because its contents are guaranteed never to change.

cards.title: array.array — Typed Arrays
cards.teaser: array.array stores values directly in a flat C array, not as Python object pointers. For large sequences of a single numeric type, it uses 4–10x less memory than list and iterates faster — without the full power of NumPy.

runs.text: Python's built-in
array
module provides
array.array
— a sequence that stores values directly as C primitives rather than as Python object pointers. You declare the type code at construction time (
for signed int,
for double, etc.), and every element is stored as that primitive type.

explanation.code:
import array, sys

lst = list(range(1_000_000))
arr = array.array('i', range(1_000_000))

print(sys.getsizeof(lst))   # ~8_000_056 bytes (8 MB — pointers only)
print(arr.buffer_info()[1] * arr.itemsize)  # 4_000_000 bytes (4 MB — ints directly)

runs.text: The API mirrors list:
append
pop
insert
, iteration, index access — all with the same Big O complexities as list. The gain is purely in memory layout: because values are stored densely as C primitives,
array.array
has better cache behavior during sequential reads and writes to disk/sockets (the
tofile
fromfile
methods are useful for binary I/O).

Use array.array when: (1) you need a large sequence of a single C-compatible numeric type, (2) you don't need NumPy's vectorized math, and (3) memory footprint or binary I/O matters. For any numeric computation, prefer NumPy — array.array doesn't support vectorized operations.

A Python list of integers is like a box of business cards where each card has an address written on it — the actual integers live elsewhere. array.array is like stamping the integers directly onto a long strip of paper with no indirection. The strip takes less space and you can scan it faster, but every value on the strip must be the same width (same type), and you can't do math on the whole strip at once without NumPy.

cards.title: NumPy Arrays — When to Use
cards.teaser: NumPy arrays store homogeneous C-typed data in a contiguous block and support vectorized math — entire operations run in compiled C with no Python loop. For numeric computation, NumPy is not a luxury; it's a 100–1000x speedup.

runs.text: A
numpy.ndarray
is a fixed-size, homogeneous, n-dimensional array backed by a contiguous C buffer. Like
array.array
it stores raw values, not Python object pointers. Unlike
array.array
, it exposes
vectorized operations
— arithmetic, comparison, and aggregation operators that operate on entire arrays in compiled C (and optionally SIMD/BLAS), bypassing the Python interpreter loop entirely.

explanation.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4], dtype=np.float64)
b = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40], dtype=np.float64)

# No Python loop — runs in compiled C
c = a * b            # [10., 40., 90., 160.]
total = a.sum()      # 10.0
normed = a / a.max() # [0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]

runs.text: Key differences from list and array.array:

items.text: — no dynamic resizing. np.append creates a new array (avoid in loops).
— arr[2:5] returns a view (O(1)), not a copy. Mutations to the view affect the original.
— operations between arrays of compatible (not necessarily equal) shapes auto-expand dimensions.
— float32, float64, int8, complex128, structured dtypes, and more.

runs.text: When to use NumPy: any numeric computation on collections larger than a few thousand elements where you'd otherwise write a Python loop. When not to use it: heterogeneous data, non-numeric types, or when you need dynamic appending — use list or deque instead. For DataFrames (labeled, mixed-type tabular data), use pandas (which uses NumPy as its backend).

A Python loop over a list is like having a warehouse worker pick up each box one at a time, read what's inside, do one operation, write it back, then move to the next box. NumPy is like a purpose-built assembly line machine that processes an entire pallet of identical boxes in one pass — the same total work happens, but the machine runs in microseconds while the warehouse worker takes seconds. That's the difference between interpreted Python loops and compiled C vectorization.
